title: Self-Edits to Weights: SEAL and the Outer RL Loop

questions.question: In SEAL, what is a "self-edit"?
options: A patch to the model's own source code that changes decoding settings such as the sampling temperature
A vector of weight deltas that the model computes in context and writes straight into its own parameter file
Generated text (restated data, augmentation flags, hyperparameters) that a fixed finetuning step turns into a weight update
A prompt prefix stored in a retrieval index and re-read at inference time instead of changing any weights at all
questions.explanation: A self-edit is an ordinary generation: implications, augmentation choices and training settings. A fixed SFT/LoRA procedure consumes it, which is what makes it both scorable text and a persistent weight change.

questions.question: Which statement about SEAL's two nested loops is correct?
options: The inner loop applies a self-edit with SFT and keeps the resulting weights; the outer loop only logs the rewards for later analysis
The inner loop applies a self-edit with SFT to score it; the outer loop (ReST-EM) fine-tunes the self-edit policy on the self-edits that scored well
The inner loop runs GRPO on the self-edit policy; the outer loop applies LoRA to the student and discards any low-reward weights
Both loops update the same weights with the same loss function; the only difference between them is the batch size each one uses
questions.explanation: Trial weights from the inner loop are thrown away; only the lesson about which self-edits improved the model survives, in the policy. SEAL used ReST-EM because GRPO-style training was unstable.

questions.question: Which reading of SEAL's paper-reported knowledge-incorporation table (v2, September 2025) is accurate?
options: SEAL beat GPT-4.1-generated data in every setting, including the 2,067-passage continued-pretraining run, by a wide margin
SEAL trailed GPT-4.1-generated data in every setting but still beat training on the raw passage alone by over ten points
SEAL matched the base model exactly in every setting, which shows that self-edits are neutral for incorporating new knowledge
SEAL beat GPT-4.1-generated data on the single-passage setting (47.0% vs 46.3%) and trailed it in the two larger continued-pretraining settings
questions.explanation: The single-passage win is the headline; in the 200- and 2,067-passage settings GPT-4.1 data led by 1.2 and 2.8 points. The policy learned per-passage data writing and the edge did not fully carry to a stream.

questions.question: Why does this lesson say SEAL is not closed-loop recursive self-improvement, despite changing its own weights?
options: Its weights change persistently, but the reward that trains the self-edit policy comes from labelled external questions; remove them and nothing is reinforced
Its weights never actually change; only a prompt is updated between cycles, so no model-level change persists from one self-edit to the next
It uses LoRA rather than full finetuning, and LoRA adapters are discarded at the end of every outer-loop round, so no improvement accumulates
It requires a stronger model such as GPT-4.1 to write the self-edits, so the loop depends entirely on an external model's judgement
questions.explanation: SEAL sits at L3 on the Liu et al. ladder: data and trainer settings change autonomously under a fixed, human-written improvement mechanism whose reward is grounded in external labels.

questions.question: In the simulator, the ReST-EM policy concentrates on implication-expand and forgetting of earlier tasks rises. What is the most accurate explanation?
options: The policy's learning rate is too high, so the inner loop diverges and the weights become effectively random on every earlier task
The reward is new-task accuracy only; a self-edit that overwrites earlier knowledge scores the same as one that does not, so nothing selects against it
Replay was on by default and the replayed examples were mislabelled, which directly damaged the model's accuracy on earlier tasks
ReST-EM keeps the lowest-reward self-edits each round, so the policy gradually learns the strategies that are worst on every task
questions.explanation: Forgetting is invisible to a new-task reward. Only a guard outside the policy (replay) or a changed reward (anchored) makes the loop pay for regression on earlier tasks.

questions.question: A team proposes letting the self-edit model also write the evaluation questions so the loop can run on unlabelled corpora. What should a safety review flag first?
options: The compute cost per self-edit would rise from 30 to 45 seconds to several hours, because writing questions is slower than finetuning
Catastrophic forgetting would disappear, because self-written questions would always cover earlier passages as well as the new one
The reward would no longer be grounded outside the system; the policy could write data and questions that confirm its current dispositions, the pattern alignment faking (12% to 78%) warns about
LoRA cannot be applied when the questions are model-written, so the pipeline would have to switch to full finetuning on every passage
questions.explanation: Context-dependent evaluation is what keeps SEAL's loop honest. Self-written evaluation removes the external anchor, which is the trade Lesson 06 analysed for self-rewarding models.
